**Trustworthy data first.** Machine learning can only be as reliable as the data it learns from, and that is where our work began. Sequencing experiments carry hidden quality problems: we showed that poor-quality samples that are unevenly distributed between patient groups, a *quality imbalance*, distort the results of a large share of published clinical RNA-seq studies ([Genome Biology, 2024](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-024-03331-6)). We develop machine-learning tools that assess data quality automatically, building on [seqQscorer](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-021-02294-2), and release [open benchmark datasets](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2604.04981) for quality control of next-generation sequencing. In the Einstein Foundation–funded project [*Erring Rigorously*](projects.qmd#erring-rigorously), we now introduce controlled errors in the wet lab to measure how they propagate into downstream analyses.

**Models that learn biology.** On the modelling side, we train and critically test foundation models for biological sequences, from DNA language models to transfer learning across peptides, metabolites and proteins. Rather than assuming that scale solves everything, we ask what these models actually learn, where standard architectures fall short, and which training objectives and benchmarks can do better. Where predictions should inform biology or the clinic, we favour interpretable models. Biologically informed neural networks such as [MiracleNet](https://doi.org/10.34133/csbj.0145) tie their predictions to known genes and pathways, for example to predict survival in lung cancer from microRNA data. Our applications come from close collaborations in immunology, cancer and vascular biology, such as the vascular-ageing project [SVITER](projects.qmd#sviter).

**Responsible and open.** Generative models that can design DNA also bring new risks. Together with partners from AI, the life sciences and policy, we develop safeguards for AI-driven biological sequence design: our [defence-in-depth framework](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78758-5) in *Nature Communications* (2026) proposes layered protections across data, models and DNA synthesis, and our [perspective](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tig.2026.04.001) in *Trends in Genetics* weighs innovation against risk in genomic AI. We share code, models and datasets openly on [GitHub](https://github.com/sprang-lab) and [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/DNA-LLM), holding back only what would pose a biosecurity risk, such as training code for viral sequence models. And because the next generation of researchers will need to work across these boundaries, we are building new teaching formats, starting with the [AIxBio: Frontiers and Futures](projects.qmd#aixbio-frontiers-and-futures) curriculum project.
